name: The Latitudinal Diversity Gradient
statement: Life is richest near the equator and thins toward the poles, but no one is sure exactly why.
statementAccent: richest near the equator and thins toward the poles
meaning: The latitudinal diversity gradient is the widespread ecological pattern that species richness is highest in the tropics, near the equator, and declines toward the poles. It holds across most major groups, from plants and insects to birds, mammals, and marine life, and through much of the fossil record, which is why it is often called ecology's oldest and most pervasive pattern. The gradient itself is one of the best-documented regularities in biology, but its cause is not: many hypotheses compete to explain it, and there is no scientific consensus, making it a central and still-open puzzle in macroecology and biogeography.
mechanism: There is no single agreed mechanism, but the leading explanations fall into a few families. Energy or productivity hypotheses hold that greater solar energy and water in the tropics support higher net productivity and so more species. Evolutionary and historical hypotheses cast the tropics as an older, larger, more stable cradle and museum of diversity, with more time for speciation, lower extinction, and higher diversification rates, and the tropical-conservatism idea that most lineages arose in the tropics and few adapt to cold. Others emphasise the greater year-round climatic stability of the tropics, their historically larger area, or more intense biotic interactions driving specialisation. Most likely several of these act together.

examples.text: From trees and beetles to birds and reef fish, richness generally rises toward the equator, the pattern that first struck naturalists exploring the tropics.
Nineteenth-century naturalists including Alexander von Humboldt, Darwin, and Alfred Russel Wallace all remarked on the tropics' extraordinary abundance of species.

The gradient is not universal: ichneumonid parasitoid wasps, some shorebirds, penguins, and certain marine and soil groups peak outside the tropics, showing it is a strong tendency, not an exceptionless law.

variants.name: Cradle and museum
variants.text: The evolutionary account in which the tropics both generate new species faster, as a cradle, and lose them more slowly, as a museum, accumulating diversity over time.

variants.name: The mid-domain effect
variants.text: A geometric null model in which randomly placed species ranges overlap most in the middle of a bounded domain, producing a diversity peak without any biological cause.

whyItMatters: The latitudinal diversity gradient is a central challenge of biodiversity science, a pattern so general that any complete theory of what controls the distribution of life must explain it. Because it ties biodiversity to climate and energy, understanding its causes bears directly on predicting how life will respond to a warming world. It has organised more than a century of research in ecology, biogeography, and evolution, and its stubborn resistance to a single explanation is itself instructive, a reminder that a robust pattern can outlast every attempt to reduce it to one cause.

working.text: anticipate that species richness generally rises toward the equator across most groups, while watching for genuine exceptions.
treat energy, evolutionary history, climatic stability, area, and biotic interactions as competing, likely complementary explanations, not a settled cause.
remember that the gradient's strength depends on the scale of measurement, being stronger at regional than at local scales.

limits: The gradient is a robust generalisation, not an exceptionless rule: some taxa, such as ichneumonid parasitoid wasps, certain shorebirds, penguins, marine mammal parasites, and soil bacteria, peak at middle or high latitudes rather than in the tropics. Its measured strength depends on how richness is defined and on spatial scale, being significantly steeper at regional than at local scales. Above all, its cause is unresolved: the many hypotheses remain contested, and the scientific consensus is that no single-cause explanation is established, so several mechanisms probably contribute together.
misreadings: It is a pattern with many candidate explanations, not a settled law with one confirmed cause, so no single hypothesis, whether energy, tropical conservatism, or area, should be presented as the answer. It is a strong statistical tendency, not an exceptionless rule, since real groups deviate from it. And it is about the number of species along latitude, sensitive to scale and definition, not a claim that every tropical location is richer than every temperate one.
origin: Recognised by nineteenth-century naturalists including Alexander von Humboldt, Charles Darwin, and Alfred Russel Wallace, and the subject of a large modern literature, including Helmut Hillebrand's 2004 meta-analysis confirming its generality across taxa.

sources.text: Latitudinal gradients in species diversity, Wikipedia. — the tropics-to-poles pattern, the competing hypotheses, the explicit lack of consensus, and the exceptions.
Hillebrand, 'On the generality of the latitudinal diversity gradient,' The American Naturalist 163(2):192-211 (2004). — the meta-analysis confirming the pattern and its scale dependence.
